# Chapter 3

## Research Methodology

The study follows the Design Science Research Methodology (DSRM) [@peffers2007design], which guides a research project through six stages: problem identification, objective formulation, design and development, demonstration, evaluation, and communication. Sections 3.2 to 3.9 apply these stages to the computational artifacts of the study.

## Subjects of the Study

The study examines three computational artifacts: the annotated disaster corpus, the model configurations, and the benchmarking laptop. The corpus contains approximately 6,000 to 10,000 Taglish disaster tweets collected and filtered from six Philippine typhoons between 2020 and 2024, yielding 1,000 to 1,700 posts per event. The six typhoons are Ulysses, Rolly, Odette, Karding, Egay, and Carina. The complete event roster appears in Appendix A. Within the corpus, the units of observation are the individual posts and their token spans.

The corpus supports three triage tasks: intent classification, urgency classification, and named entity recognition. Every post is annotated jointly across the three tasks, following joint-task annotation practice [@sheth2025comilingua]. Joint annotation ensures that every model configuration receives identical inputs. Each post carries one intent label, one urgency label, and zero or more entity spans.

Two of the label sets are adapted from established taxonomies. The intent categories follow the HumAID humanitarian taxonomy [@alam2021humaid]. The urgency levels start from the binary urgent and non-urgent categories of prior Philippine disaster work [@ermino2022urgency] and expand them into three levels, in line with the multi-level priority convention of TREC-IS [@wang2021transformer]. The complete inventory of task labels appears in Appendix A.

For named entity recognition, the study annotates two entity types: LOCATION and INFRASTRUCTURE. LOCATION follows standard named entity recognition conventions [@tjongkimsang2003conll]. INFRASTRUCTURE is the span-level counterpart of the infrastructure and utility damage category of HumAID. When two entity spans overlap, the longest span is retained, following the CoNLL-2003 treatment of overlapping entities [@tjongkimsang2003conll].

Code-switching varies widely across the corpus, so each post is assigned to one of three linguistic strata: Tagalog-dominant, Mixed Taglish, or English-dominant. The assignment is based on the Code-Mixing Index [@gamback2016comparing], a score that quantifies how much a text mixes two languages. The index offers no default thresholds, so the stratum boundaries are fixed in the annotation guidelines before labeling begins.

Labeling is carried out by two bilingual annotators fluent in Tagalog and English. Before the corpus is frozen, both annotators independently label a shared subsample so that consistency can be measured. Section 3.5 describes this step in detail. The choice of agreement measure depends on the task type. For the two categorical tasks, agreement is quantified with Cohen's kappa [@cohen1960coefficient], and a task passes when its kappa reaches at least .61, the lower bound of the substantial-agreement band [@landis1977measurement]. For named entity recognition, agreement is measured with entity-level F1 [@tjongkimsang2003conll], and the task passes at .75 or higher, a level comparable to the entity agreement of published annotated corpora [@campillos2018merlot]. Any disagreement is resolved through consensus adjudication, following the HumAID protocol [@alam2021humaid].

The study implements one multi-task triage architecture [@caruana1997multitask] and trains it under the five multi-task training methods listed in Chapter 1. Every multi-task configuration is compared against three dedicated single-task baselines, one per task, following multi-task benchmarking practice [@weld2023survey]. The five training methods are (a) equal weighting [@caruana1997multitask], (b) tuned static weighting [@gama2025uniform], (c) loss balancing through GradNorm [@chen2018gradnorm], (d) gradient surgery through PCGrad [@yu2020gradient], and (e) a combination of loss balancing and gradient surgery. In the combined method, PCGrad is applied to the per-task gradients of the GradNorm-weighted losses.

The architecture couples a shared pretrained encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M [@aisingapore2026sealion], with three task-specific heads: a token-classification head for named entity recognition and two sequence-classification heads for intent and urgency classification. All five multi-task training methods use this same encoder and set of heads. Each single-task baseline also uses the same encoder and the corresponding task-head architecture. This design holds model architecture constant across the multi-task methods and aligns each single-task baseline with its corresponding multi-task task head.

All training and profiling run on a single dedicated commodity laptop so that the execution environment stays constant. The next section describes how the data are partitioned for evaluation.

## Sampling Technique

The evaluation targets out-of-domain generalization: the ability to make triage predictions for posts from a typhoon event not represented in the training data. The study therefore employs leave-one-disaster-out (LODO) cross-validation across the six typhoon events ($K = 6$), following held-out event evaluation practice in crisis informatics [@seeberger2025generalizing]. Each fold holds out one typhoon event as the test set, while the remaining $K - 1$ events form the training pool. By holding out entire events, LODO reduces the risk that models rely on event-specific keywords, local place names, or temporal markers rather than patterns that generalize across disasters.

Within each fold, a 15% development split is drawn from the training pool. The split is stratified jointly across typhoon events and task labels [@sechidis2011stratification], so that rare label combinations remain represented. The same fixed split is used for every model configuration. It provides a common basis for validation, early stopping, and hyperparameter tuning. The held-out event is never accessed during training or checkpoint selection.

To control for stochastic optimization and initialization variance, each model configuration is trained across $S = 5$ random seeds for every fold [@reimers2017reporting]. All seed runs share identical batch sequences, learning rate schedules, and early stopping rules. Performance scores are averaged across the five seeds within each fold. The typhoon event is the unit of analysis.

## Instruments to Be Used

Predictive performance is evaluated with the task metrics defined in Section 3.7. Serving efficiency is measured with the instruments listed in @tbl-instruments.

Latency trials use batch size one, matching the SingleStream scenario standardized by MLPerf Inference [@reddi2020mlperf]. End-to-end latency is timed with the monotonic clock `time.perf_counter_ns` [@python2026time]. The multi-task model is profiled in two modes: its three task heads are executed sequentially or concurrently. Each single-task baseline is also profiled separately. Peak allocated GPU memory is recorded with `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated` [@paszke2019pytorch]. Peak host memory is estimated from resident set size (RSS) samples collected with `psutil`. Measurements use pinned versions of PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, and the CUDA runtime.

| Instrument | Measured Property | Implementation Tool |
|---|---|---|
| Monotonic latency timer | Single-stream end-to-end request latency | `time.perf_counter_ns` |
| Framework memory counter | Peak allocated GPU memory | `torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated` |
| Process memory monitor | Peak host resident set size (RSS) | `psutil` |

: Measurement Instruments and Measured Properties {#tbl-instruments}

*Note.* RSS = resident set size.

Several established benchmarking tools were considered but were not adopted as complete suites. MLPerf Inference [@reddi2020mlperf] evaluates predefined reference models on standardized hardware rather than custom multi-task models on a single laptop. Its SingleStream scenario and warm-up convention nevertheless inform the measurement protocol. Inference optimization engines such as TensorRT and ONNX Runtime are also excluded because compiler optimization would add another factor to the comparison. The study focuses on computational differences between single-task and multi-task designs. Edge and mobile profiling tools target hardware outside the laptop testbed.

## Procedure of Data Gathering

Data gathering proceeds in four steps: collection, cleaning, annotation, and execution.

The first step establishes the collection windows. For each typhoon, the study consults the official bulletins of the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) and records the landfall timestamp. For events without direct landfall, the officially recorded onset of impact serves as the anchor. A collection window is then fixed from 24 hours before to 72 hours after the anchor, following event-anchored collection practice in crisis informatics [@olteanu2014crisislex]. Posts are retrieved through research archives and authorized tweet hydration, following event-based crisis tweet collection practice [@alam2021humaid]. The search queries combine typhoon names, official hashtags, and disaster-related keywords in Tagalog and English.

The second step cleans and normalizes the raw posts before they enter the machine learning pipelines. Duplicate posts are removed, and non-text content such as media attachments is excluded. Text normalization standardizes whitespace variations and character encodings. Posts that fail automatic language identification or Code-Mixing Index screening are logged and excluded from the corpus. Privacy protection is part of this step: to uphold the Data Privacy Act of 2012 (Republic Act No. 10173) [@ra10173], user handles, full names, telephone numbers, URLs containing account parameters, and non-public metadata are stripped, and each post receives an anonymous internal identifier.

The third step is annotation. The two bilingual annotators first work through a shared practice batch to identify linguistic ambiguities and refine the annotation guidelines. Once the guidelines are finalized, they divide the corpus and independently label their assigned posts across all three triage tasks. They then independently label the same stratified subsample, which contains at least 20% of the corpus and includes posts from both production subsets. During this second round, neither annotator has access to the original labels. This procedure follows partial double-annotation practice [@bamman2020coref]. Inter-annotator agreement is evaluated on the common subsample using the criteria and thresholds in Section 3.2. If a task falls below its target threshold, the guidelines are revised, and all affected instances are re-annotated. Any remaining disagreements are resolved through consensus adjudication before the corpus is frozen.

The fourth step is execution. Once the annotated corpus is frozen, the six LODO folds and their 15% development splits are generated as described in Section 3.3. Before training, an automated check records class support in each training, development, and test partition. It also verifies that each held-out event is excluded from training and development. The check does not require every class to appear in every partition. A class absent from a held-out event is marked as not observed. A class present in the test event but absent from the training data is flagged and reported. Model training then runs on the laptop under the training orchestrator of Section 3.8.1. Each configuration produces predictions on its held-out event and then undergoes efficiency profiling with the instruments of Section 3.4. The profiling follows MLPerf benchmarking practice [@reddi2020mlperf]. For each serving condition, unmeasured warm-up passes run until execution reaches steady state, followed by 100 timed batch-size-one trials. The monotonic timer measures end-to-end inference latency with explicit device synchronization. Peak allocated GPU memory and host resident set size are recorded for each trial. The GPU peak-memory counter is reset between trials. Because the five training methods share one architecture, efficiency is measured three ways: the multi-task model under sequential head execution, the same model under concurrent head execution, and each single-task baseline.

To ensure reproducibility and eliminate manual transcription, all predictive performance scores and hardware measurements are written directly by the execution scripts into structured JSON manifests and CSV files. These logs serve as the inputs to the statistical testing and data analysis that follow.

## Statistical Treatment

The inferential analysis accounts for the hierarchical structure of the experimental design [@dror2018hitchhiker]. The held-out typhoon event is the unit of analysis ($N = K = 6$), and the significance level is $\alpha = .05$. The hypotheses stated in Chapter 1 compare the five multi-task training methods on fold-level macro negative transfer. For each method and held-out event, F1 scores are first averaged across the five seeds. The task-level drops relative to the corresponding single-task baselines are then averaged across the three tasks to produce one macro negative-transfer score. Section 3.7 gives the formal definition.

**Null hypothesis ($H_0$).** There is no statistically significant difference in negative transfer among the five training methods on unseen typhoon events.

**Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$).** At least one of the five training methods differs significantly in negative transfer from at least one of the others on unseen typhoon events.

The null hypothesis is tested with a Friedman test that compares the five methods across the six held-out events. For each event, the test uses one fold-level macro negative-transfer score per method. The null distribution is estimated by Monte Carlo permutation. In each iteration, the five method labels are shuffled within every fold, and the Friedman statistic is recalculated. This process is repeated for $B = 100{,}000$ iterations. Rejecting the omnibus test is sufficient to support $H_1$, because the alternative hypothesis claims only that at least one method differs from at least one of the others.

After the omnibus test, the ten pairwise comparisons provide descriptive rankings of the methods. Each pair is compared using its six fold-level macro negative-transfer differences in a two-sided exact sign-flipping permutation test. Both unadjusted and Holm-Bonferroni-adjusted *p*-values [@holm1979simple] are reported for every comparison. With six folds, the exact test has $2^6 = 64$ possible sign patterns, so the smallest attainable two-sided *p*-value is $2/64 = .031$. This minimum exceeds the first Holm-Bonferroni threshold ($\alpha/10 = .005$). Therefore, no pairwise comparison can reach significance after correction. The adjusted *p*-values are reported for completeness but cannot support a significant pairwise conclusion under this design. Whenever the omnibus test rejects, the method with the lowest fold-level macro negative transfer is descriptively identified as the method that best mitigates negative transfer.

## Data Analysis

The analysis reports one set of measures for the classification tasks and another for named entity recognition. For the intent and urgency classification tasks, the study computes classification accuracy alongside macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1. Accuracy counts the proportion of correctly labeled test posts. Precision, recall, and F1 are derived per class $c$ and then macro-averaged across the class set, which gives every class equal weight regardless of frequency.

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{1}{N_{\text{posts}}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{posts}}} \mathbb{I}(\hat{y}_i = y_i)$$

$$P_c = \frac{\text{TP}_c}{\text{TP}_c + \text{FP}_c}, \quad R_c = \frac{\text{TP}_c}{\text{TP}_c + \text{FN}_c}, \quad F1_c = \frac{2 P_c R_c}{P_c + R_c}$$

$$\text{Macro-F1} = \frac{1}{|C|} \sum_{c \in C} F1_c$$

Named entity recognition is scored differently because it is a span-level task rather than a post-level task. The measure is micro-averaged entity-level F1 under the strict CoNLL-2003 evaluation criteria [@tjongkimsang2003conll]. Token labels are encoded in BIO tagging and decoded into spans before scoring. Under this matching rule, a predicted entity span counts as a true positive only when its start offset, end offset, and entity type all match the reference annotation exactly.

A single composite score captures overall triage performance across all three tasks. The overall triage score is the unweighted mean of the three per-task F1 scores, combining the macro-averaged F1 of the two classification tasks with the micro-averaged entity-level F1 of named entity recognition.

$$\overline{\text{F1}} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \text{F1}_t$$

Per-stratum reporting shows model performance across the three code-switching groups defined in Section 3.2. For each random seed, held-out predictions are pooled across the six folds, so every annotated post receives one prediction per seed. Task metrics are calculated separately for each stratum and then averaged across the five seeds.

Negative transfer quantifies the performance degradation of the multi-task model on a task relative to the single-task baseline trained for that task alone [@wu2020information]. For each task $t$, F1 scores are averaged across the five seeds within each fold before the drop is calculated. Averaging the three task-level drops yields that method's fold-level macro negative-transfer score, which is used in the tests of Section 3.6.

$$\text{NT}_t = \text{F1}_{\text{STL}, t} - \text{F1}_{\text{MTL}, t}, \quad \overline{\text{NT}} = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} \text{NT}_t$$

Serving efficiency is quantified through latency, throughput, and memory usage. Single-stream inference latency is expressed in milliseconds. Here, $L_i$ denotes the end-to-end latency of timed trial $i$ across $N_{\text{trials}}$ repeated trials, and latency is reported as the mean and standard deviation. Throughput is derived from the elapsed time of the same trials and is expressed as posts processed per second.

$$\bar{L} = \frac{1}{N_{\text{trials}}} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{trials}}} L_i, \quad \text{SD}_L = \sqrt{\frac{1}{N_{\text{trials}} - 1} \sum_{i=1}^{N_{\text{trials}}} (L_i - \bar{L})^2}$$

$$\text{Throughput} = \frac{N_{\text{posts}}}{t_{\text{elapsed}}}$$

Memory usage is recorded in megabytes and captures both peak allocated GPU memory and peak host resident set size. Relative resource reduction compares the shared multi-task model with its three heads executed concurrently against a sequential workload that runs the three single-task baselines one after another. Latency and memory reductions are calculated separately. The multi-task model's sequential-head measurements are reported as a separate serving condition. All metrics are computed automatically by the research software system detailed in Section 3.8.

$$\text{Reduction} = 1 - \frac{\text{Resource}_{\text{concurrent}}}{\text{Resource}_{\text{sequential}}}$$

## Software System Description

### System Structure

The benchmarking pipeline, the five training methods, and the serving workflows are integrated into one research software system. The architecture diagram in @fig-system-architecture shows its data pipeline, shared model core, execution orchestrators, and telemetry outputs. The system is organized around three modular subsystems: the data pipeline, the model core, and the execution orchestrators.

The data pipeline handles post ingestion, deduplication, language identification, Code-Mixing Index screening, text normalization, and stratum assignment. When processing completes, it saves an immutable corpus store. Immutability guarantees that every experimental fold operates on identical inputs. The model core organizes the shared encoder and the three task-specific heads specified in Section 3.2. Under multi-task configurations, it routes the shared representations from the encoder into all three heads simultaneously. Under single-task baselines, the same encoder feeds a single head.

![System architecture and data flow for the Taglish disaster triage benchmarking pipeline.](figures/fig-3-5-system-architecture){#fig-system-architecture}

The operational workflow is coordinated by two execution components: the training orchestrator and the serving orchestrator. The training orchestrator executes the benchmarking grid across eight model configurations, six folds, and five random seeds. The eight configurations are the three single-task baselines and the five training methods. All configurations share identical computational budgets and explore a common hyperparameter search space over learning rates and weight decay values, so no method receives a tuning advantage [@xin2022current]. For the tuned static weighting method, the per-task loss weights are additionally optimized on the development split of each fold over a pre-specified weight grid.

Training failures are handled by a fixed restart policy. A run that displays loss divergence or collapse to the majority class is automatically restarted once with the same seed. A recurring failure prompts manual inspection, and a run is excluded only for persistent loss divergence or repeated out-of-memory failure. The serving orchestrator manages the profiling routines and measures serving efficiency across sequential head execution, concurrent head execution, and the single-task baselines.

### Use Cases

The system supports both experimental benchmarking and prospective deployment in disaster response. System operations are organized around three actors. The response analyst is the humanitarian practitioner who filters posts by urgency, intent, or location and examines ranked lists of urgent posts with extracted locations and confidence scores. The system operator is the researcher or technical administrator who configures, executes, and monitors the multi-task training runs and hardware profiling experiments. The MLOps worker is an automated agent responsible for evaluating saved model checkpoints and writing structured logs. Each use case is specified in @tbl-usecases, and the UML use case diagram is illustrated in @fig-use-cases.

| Use Case Category | Use Case | Use Case Description |
|---|---|---|
| Triage support | View triaged disaster posts | The response analyst filters posts by urgency, intent, or location and receives a ranked list of urgent posts with extracted locations and confidence scores. |
| Model training | Train model configuration | The system operator trains one of the eight model configurations on a chosen fold and seed, and the system saves checkpoints and training logs automatically. |
| Efficiency profiling | Measure inference speed and memory | The system operator loads a trained configuration, runs unmeasured warm-up passes, executes 100 timed batch-size-one trials, and records latency and memory usage for each serving condition. |
| Evaluation and logging | Evaluate trained configurations | The MLOps worker scores saved checkpoints on the held-out typhoon event and registers the results in the execution manifest. |

## Testing and Evaluation

Before full-scale training begins, the software pipeline and measurement instruments undergo systematic verification under a continuous integration framework. Every verification test must pass. Together, these tests prevent numerical bugs and data transformation errors from propagating through the benchmark.

The unit testing suite targets each component in isolation using deterministic synthetic fixtures. Five tests make up the suite. The first test checks that tokenization followed by detokenization reproduces each benchmark fixture exactly, except for changes allowed by the documented normalization rules. The second test verifies that per-task mean-reduced loss calculations match hand-calculated reference values within floating-point tolerances. The third test verifies the output shapes of the three heads: the named entity recognition head produces token-level entity-class logits, while the intent and urgency heads produce post-level class logits. The fourth test validates the Code-Mixing Index implementation against hand-calculated cases covering monolingual Tagalog, monolingual English, balanced code-switched text, and lexical borrowing. The fifth test checks partition integrity for each random seed by pooling predictions across the six held-out folds. The pooled predictions must include every corpus post exactly once, with no omissions or duplicates. The test also confirms that each held-out event is excluded from training in its corresponding fold.

Integration and stress tests follow the unit tests. Their purpose is to confirm that the individual subsystems operate together under sustained computational workloads. An end-to-end smoke test executes a complete miniature cycle of model training, checkpoint saving, metric scoring, and log creation, and validates all generated CSV and JSON output files against predefined schemas. Latency scaling is then profiled across expanding batch sizes to evaluate system behavior under increased serving loads. During sustained inference runs, GPU core and memory temperatures are logged to detect thermal throttling that could skew timing records. Finally, peak GPU memory and host resident set size are audited across consecutive evaluation passes to confirm the absence of memory leaks.

The research artifact is evaluated against the ISO/IEC 25010 software product quality standard [@iso25010]. Three dimensions apply. Performance efficiency is addressed through the single-stream latency and peak memory usage benchmarks. Reliability is enforced through the run-integrity restart policy, schema validation, and seed-controlled reproducibility. Portability is satisfied through pinned environment manifests and an open-source dissemination package. The remaining quality dimensions are documented as non-applicable, because the artifact is a single-investigator research benchmark rather than an interactive commercial product.
